extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and legal scholars handling infringement remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for when courts of equity (injunctions, accounts) or courts of law (damages, actions at law) provide adequate relief in patent-infringement disputes, and related rules on who may sue and what remedies are appropriate. Includes when discovery, accounting of profits, and injunctions are available or inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No adequate remedy at law for prevention of future infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate remedy at law does not exist in any case where future infringements are to be prevented; future infringements can be prevented only by an injunction issuing out of chancery, and to this relief the plaintiff is entitled whenever he has reason to apprehend a violation of his rights by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: (1) where the plaintiff has an established license fee collectible at law (no injunction needed); (2) where the infringement has been finally abandoned by the defendant or has become impossible through expiration of the patent. If no established license fee exists, or the fee could not be collected (e.g., defendant insolvent), equity will restrain the defendant and afford further relief. (See §1088 and cited cases: Motte v. Bennett; Sherman v. Nutt; Brick v. Staten Island R.R. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity required where injured party is not legal owner
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of law can give complete redress for past infringements only where the injured party is the legal owner of the patent and compensation can be measured by actual damage; a plaintiff who is equitably interested but not the legal owner cannot maintain a suit for damages and must resort to equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations requiring equity: purchaser who has not received conveyance; equitable assignee; heir or devisee where personal representative holds patent in trust; licensee whose exclusive privileges are invaded; or other cases where complete relief cannot be secured without asserting equitable interest. (See §1069, §1089 and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction when discovery is necessary or defense rests on equitable grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity may assume jurisdiction to compel discovery when data essential to computation of compensation or other material facts are within defendant's knowledge and cannot be ascertained except through his disclosure; likewise, when defendant's defense rests on equitable grounds that would lead to circuity of action, equity may entertain the plaintiff's claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will take jurisdiction to compel discovery and then retain it until entire relief is afforded. Examples: suits involving discovery against licensees; cases where defense would require the plaintiff to pursue a separate equitable claim. (See §1090 and cited cases: Root v. Lake Shore & Mich. Southern R.R. Co.; Perry v. Coming.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits is ordinarily incidental to an injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to an account of profits in infringement cases is not ipso facto an equitable remedy but is ordinarily incidental to the right to an injunction or other equitable relief; chancery acquires no jurisdiction solely from the fact that the defendant has made profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although historically debated, the Supreme Court holds that a naked bill for account of profits cannot be sustained; however, where the nature of the account renders equitable interposition necessary (e.g., complex matters, discovery needs), chancery jurisdiction may exist. Parties should pursue account at law when practicable; equity reserved for cases law cannot adequately resolve. (See §1091; Stevens v. Gladding; Root v. Lake Shore & Mich. Southern R.R. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether defendant's gains exceeding plaintiff's loss confers equity jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the defendant's pecuniary gains from wrongful use, exceeding the plaintiff's loss, are alone sufficient to confer equity jurisdiction for an accounting has been disputed; some courts held yes, but the Supreme Court negatived the proposition that profits alone always create equitable jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory history (acts of 1790–1870) and policy arguments support allowing recovery of gains and savings; yet the settled rule is that profits do not automatically create equity jurisdiction. Instead, equity may grant an account when equitable relief (e.g., injunction, discovery) or the nature of the accounting makes legal remedies inadequate. Consider bringing account actions at law where possible; equity reserved for exceptions. (See §1091 and extended discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where remedy at law is adequate, equity has no jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity will not intervene where the remedy at law is adequate — e.g., when plaintiff's right to compensation and its amount can be made manifest by proceedings incident to a jury trial in a court of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule repeated: equity is appropriate only where legal remedies are inadequate (e.g., to prevent future infringements, compel discovery, protect equitable interests). Courts should prefer legal remedies when they afford complete redress. (See multiple sections and cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere intricacy of an account does not confer equity jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere intricacy of an account does not give equity jurisdiction; equity intervenes only when the remedy at law is less adequate than that in equity for settling accounts of profits or receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases hold that complexity alone is insufficient; but where an account can be more readily settled in equity than at law (e.g., necessity of discovery or compulsion), equity may assume jurisdiction. (See Creamer v. Bowers; Kilbourn v. Sunderland.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor's remedies for royalties and limitations on equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensor cannot sue in equity to recover royalties; where the licensor grants licenses to certain persons only, he may sue an infringer at law for the license fee or damages, or in equity for an injunction with profits and damages in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will not annul a license on the ground that the licensee does not pay royalties or make required reports. If licensor has merely the right to royalties, his remedy is typically at law. (See Trandall v. Piano Mfg. Co.; Brews­ter v. Tuthill Spring Co.; other cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction during pendency of patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will issue under the Patent Law against one who infringes pending the application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will not enjoin use during pendency of application (see Rein v. Clayton). If plaintiff's rights require equity and other grounds exist, courts may still take jurisdiction in appropriate cases. (See §1088 notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where defendant no longer able to infringe, injunction unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant is no longer able to infringe (e.g., by death or ceasing production) no injunction is required and incident remedies (like account) may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: injunction cannot issue against deceased defendant's executor absent proof of infringement by executor; thus ancillary equitable relief that depends on injunction/discovery also fails. (See Draper v. Hudson and discussion in §1091.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where infringement is breach of contract, remedy at law is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the infringement is a breach of contract — and the contract determines compensation for the plaintiff's injury — the sum is recoverable at law and equitable interference cannot be invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases sustain bills for accounts under contract relating to patents (even where patent expired during suit), but when rights derive from contractual provisions the action at law for breach is generally adequate. (See references to bills sustained for account under contracts; Magic Ruffle Co. v. Elm City Co.; Eureka Co. v. Bailey Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity protects equitable interests and may afford complete relief specific to those rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a plaintiff's sole or primary rights are equitable (e.g., equitable title, trust rights), equity may interfere and administer complete relief according to the nature of those rights and how they are affected by infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable owners who cannot sue at law may obtain injunctions, discovery, and accounting suited to protect equitable interests; if equitable owner can sue at law in name of legal owner and obtain adequate relief, equity has no jurisdiction. (See §1069, §1090 notes and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent expiration before suit commenced — scope of equitable relief for post-expiration uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity can entertain an action for infringement instituted after expiration of the patent when the infringing act is the use or sale of articles that were made during the life of the patent for that purpose; equity may restrain such use as in suits begun during patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringing acts after expiration are limited to use/sale of articles made during patent life; injunctions may be necessary in those instances. If the plaintiff has only an equitable interest and legal title situation prevents legal remedy, equity may intervene. (See §1092 and cross-references to §908 and notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court should prefer actions at law for accounts where parties and transactions permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the number of parties and the nature of transactions permit, the plaintiff should bring his action for account in a court of law; equity should be used when the law cannot adjust conflicting claims or when equitable jurisdiction is warranted by the nature of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested practical rule: require plaintiffs to litigate accounts at law when feasible, reserving chancery for situations needing equitable procedures (discovery, prevention of multiplicity of suits, complex fiduciary-like matters). Consider treble damages and judicial discretion in increasing awards where profits exceed plaintiff's loss. (See concluding paragraphs of §1091.)
